title: Agent Pub/Sub in Twelve Lines of Go, With the Broker Built In
description: Every Pilot daemon runs a small pub/sub broker on port 1002. Subscribe and publish from Go with the eventstream package, or from the shell with pilotctl.

The Problem with Brokers for Agents
Message brokers are built for microservices running in the same data center. They assume:
All producers and consumers can reach the broker over TCP
The broker runs on infrastructure you control
You can manage topics, partitions, and consumer groups
You need persistence, replay, and exactly-once delivery

Agent networks break most of these assumptions. Agents sit behind NAT. They run on laptops, VMs, and edge devices. They join and leave dynamically. And most agent communication is fire-and-forget: metrics, status updates, task completion signals. You do not need Kafka's durability guarantees for a CPU utilization event that is stale in 10 seconds.
topic routing between agents that can reach each other
, over connections that work through NAT, with encryption that does not require certificate management. Port 1002 gives you that, with one condition: one of the daemons acts as the broker.
There is still a broker. It is just not a separate service: it is part of the Pilot daemon you already run. The rules are short, and all of them come from the broker's source (
The first event on a connection is its subscription.
Its topic is either an exact topic name or
for every topic. Every later event on that connection is a publication.
and nothing else. There are no prefix wildcards:
A publication goes to every subscriber of its topic plus every
subscriber, except the connection that sent it.
Nothing is stored. A subscriber that is not connected when an event is published never sees it.

Each publishing connection may send 100 events per second, with bursts of up to 200; events over the limit are dropped. A topic can have up to 1,000 subscribers. Topic names are capped at 1,024 bytes and payloads at 16 MiB.
A failed write is retried once. After three failed or timed-out (5 s) writes in a row, the broker closes that subscriber's connection.

Who can connect depends on the hub daemon's visibility. Port 1002 is reached over a Pilot tunnel, and a private daemon (the default) only accepts tunnels from peers it trusts or shares a network with. So a private hub serves only agents that have completed a
with it. A public daemon accepts tunnels from anyone, and the broker's default topic policy allows any topic, so keep a hub private unless you want an open channel.

Event streams are not just for metrics. You can build multi-stage workflows where each agent watches for a completion event and starts the next stage.

Here is Agent 2 as an example. The others follow the same pattern.

Each agent is independent. Agent 2 does not know about Agent 3. It just publishes a completion event. If Agent 3 is down, the event is lost: this is fire-and-forget pub/sub, not a durable queue. When Agent 3 comes back and subscribes again, it picks up new events. If a lost job matters, have the stage that owns it re-publish until the next stage confirms, or keep jobs in a store and use events only as wake-up signals.

has publish and subscribe commands that speak the same protocol.

fields.code:
# Terminal 1: subscribe to CPU metrics on the hub
pilotctl subscribe <hub-address> metrics.cpu

# Terminal 2: publish a CPU metric
pilotctl publish <hub-address> metrics.cpu --data '{"host":"agent-a","percent":73.2}'

# Terminal 3: publish a memory metric (terminal 1 does not see this one)
pilotctl publish <hub-address> metrics.memory --data '{"host":"agent-b","alloc_mb":256}'

children.text: The hub can be given as an address or, once you trust it, as its hostname. Use the CLI to try out your topic names before writing Go code.
a replacement for Kafka in all scenarios. You still need a real broker when:
Events must survive restarts. Pilot's stream keeps nothing. If the subscriber is offline when an event is published, that event is gone.
You need to re-process events from a specific offset. There is no event log.
Multiple instances of the same subscriber need to split the workload. Pilot delivers every event to every subscriber of its topic, not to one of many.
The broker gives at-most-once delivery. Events published during a disconnect, over the rate limit, or to a subscriber whose writes keep failing are dropped.
Each publishing connection is limited to 100 events per second (bursts of 200). Workloads far beyond that belong on infrastructure built for them.
If you depend on topic wildcards or hierarchies, use a broker that has them.
But here is the question to ask yourself: does your agent system actually need any of those? Most agent event traffic is:
Task completion signals (at-most-once is fine when the application handles retries)
Metrics (stale data is replaced by fresh data)
Coordination signals ("I am ready", "start next phase")
For these patterns, the broker already in your Pilot daemon is often enough. Save Kafka for when you actually need Kafka.

Start with the CLI to try out your topic names. Move to Go when you need programmatic control. Pick a hub daemon every agent can trust, open one subscription per exact topic, and publish completion events to chain stages. When a topic outgrows the rate limit or needs durability, move that topic to a dedicated broker and keep Pilot for the coordination traffic.
